paras.text: Malaria transmission is perennial and low, with the peak season coinciding with the rainy season, which has historically been between November and March. Malaria case incidence in 2021 was 121 cases per 1000, according to routine surveillance data reported in the national health management information system (HMIS). Chidenguele has seven rural health facilities (HFs) and nine community health workers (CHWs). Monthly malaria case counts are reported by each HF and are electronically submitted to the HMIS using the District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2) (https://dhis2.org) at the district level. To improve the accuracy of the reported data, routine data quality assessments have been implemented since 2019 [14].

Satellite imagery (SI) maps were used throughout the campaign to aid planning, implementation and progress monitoring. Prior to the implementation, all HHs in the target area were enumerated and mapped using Reveal® (Akros, https://revealprecision.com/). The target area was divided into equally sized delivery areas, which were later allocated to the fieldworker teams. During the implementation phase, the maps were transferred into an in-field application, which, combined with Global Positioning System navigation, guided the teams in the field to their assigned areas. When the fieldworkers reached each mapped structure, they were able to validate whether it was an eligible HH for the pMDA or not. If they found HHs that did not appear on the map, they were able to add them, providing an accurate HH target denominator. Fieldworkers marked eligible HHs on the map based on their visitation status as “completed”, “not or partially completed”, or “refused to participate/long-term absence”. This information was additionally transferred onto dashboards for real-time monitoring of the campaign’s progress. After field verification, the final number of eligible HHs identified in the administrative post of Chidenguele through SI was 14,045. Based on this number of HHs, the estimated population according to SI estimates was 57,304. This calculation assumes an average HH size of 4.08 members, derived from the data collected during the second round.

A HH survey was conducted three weeks after the end of pMDA2 in a sample of 770 randomly selected individuals using multistage cluster sampling. Using the HH Reveal map from pMDA2, areas with the same number of HHs were created, from which 154 were randomly selected. Within each of the selected areas, 5 HHs were randomly selected, and within each HH one individual was randomly chosen. All HHs and individuals were eligible to be selected, including those not visited during the pMDA. To maximize the chances of finding the selected individuals, HHs were visited up to three times. If the selected individual refused to participate in the survey or was absent after three visits, a different HH member was randomly selected. If the individual was too young to respond independently, a parent was asked to answer on his/her behalf. However, participants were encouraged to respond for themselves whenever possible, without influence from others. The sample size was estimated assuming the different outcomes would have a prevalence of 50% (to provide the most conservative estimate), with a confidence level of 95%, a margin of error of 5% and a design effect of 2. After obtaining informed consent, a standardized electronic questionnaire using Open Data Kit (ODK, https://getodk.org/) was filled out for each participant by trained fieldworkers who were not involved in the pMDA implementation. Data were transferred into Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap, https://www.project-redcap.org/) tools hosted at CISM’s server [15]. Data were collected on sociodemographics, participation in the pMDA, acceptability, and AEs.

Mozambique was the fifth country worldwide with the highest burden of malaria cases in 2024, accounting for 3.6% of global cases [1]. In 2022, the average prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum (P. falciparum) infection in children under five years of age was 32.3%, although transmission intensity in the country is very heterogeneous, ranging from 0.3% in Maputo province – which is targeted for elimination – to 54.7% in Nampula province [2]. The National Malaria Control Program (NMCP) aims to reduce the burden of malaria in the high transmission areas and sustain progress toward elimination in the south, and revert the increasing trend in malaria cases observed between 2019 and 2023 [3, 4].

In view of the stagnating progress in malaria control over the past decade, the World Health Organization (WHO) has highlighted the need for a significant expansion in the use of chemoprevention, which is a key component of the WHO-recommended package of interventions to reduce transmission and prevent morbidity and mortality, alongside vector control and diagnostic testing and treatment [5]. Chemoprevention consists of full therapeutic courses of antimalarial medicines administered regardless of infection status at predefined intervals to treat existing infections and prevent new ones [6]. When all population age groups in a defined geographical area are targeted, the intervention is known as mass drug administration (MDA), which has historically been an important component of malaria control and elimination strategies [7]. In the 2022 WHO’s updated chemoprevention guidelines, the use of MDA was recommended to reduce disease burden in moderate to high transmission settings and in emergency settings, as well as to reduce transmission of P. falciparum in very low to low transmission settings, alongside good coverage of case management, vector control and surveillance [8]. To achieve significant impact, MDA campaigns should achieve at least 80% coverage of the target population, which requires a high level of community engagement to enhance community participation, acceptance and adherence, as well as appropriate delivery strategies to reach all households (HHs) in the targeted area [9].

Several MDA campaigns have been implemented in Mozambique in recent years. Between 2015 and 2018 the Magude Project implemented MDA and intensified vector control (long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS)) in a low transmission area in the south of the country [10, 11]. MDA campaigns for burden reduction in Cabo Delgado Province, located in the north of the country and hit by conflict, have also been implemented by the NMCP since 2021.

Given that the updated WHO recommendations provide more flexibility to countries to adapt the implementation of MDA to their specific context [6], it was important to understand the contextual factors that would affect MDA coverage and design an implementation strategy adapted to the Mozambican context, as no guidelines for programmatic MDA (pMDA) (i.e., deployed as a routine activity implemented by the NMCP through the national health system) were available in the country. In this context, we aimed to develop, pilot and evaluate an implementation strategy and monitoring plan for pMDA in Mozambique. This article presents the coverage and impact evaluation of the pMDA campaign. Additional implementation outcomes are presented elsewhere [12].

The pMDA was piloted and evaluated in the administrative post of Chidenguele (Manjacaze District, Gaza Province). It is one of the five administrative posts in the district, a rural coastal area located in southern Mozambique (24° 04’ south, 33° 56’ east). In 2021, the estimated population in the administrative post as provided by the district health directorate (based on the 2017 national census) was 59,271 individuals living in 14,818 HHs (assuming 4 people per HH). The area has several lakes and ponds surrounded by sandy soils and coastal dunes [13].

Coverage was assessed using the programmatic data collected during the pMDA implementation as well as through a community-based cross-sectional HH survey (HH survey). Additional implementation outcomes were evaluated following a mixed-methods approach and are reported elsewhere [12].

Implementation outcomes are presented as proportions calculated from programmatic data (involving the total population) and data collected during the HH survey. For the latter, 95% confidence intervals (CI) were computed. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata, version 18.0 [16].

A cITS analysis with a comparison group was conducted to evaluate the impact of the pMDA campaign on malaria incidence. We assessed whether the pre-intervention to post-intervention change in malaria incidence just after the implementation of the pMDA was different in the intervention group versus the comparison group (level or intercept change) and whether the change in the incidence trend over the 22 months following the intervention (compared to the two years pre-intervention) was different in the intervention group versus the comparison group (trend or slope change) [17].

We used a generalized estimating equations model with negative binomial distribution and an autoregressive correlation structure, adjusted for covariates. The interruption, indicating when the pMDA was implemented, was included for December 2022 to February 2023. The pre-intervention period was from November 2020 to November 2022 and the post-intervention period from March 2023 to December 2024. Statistical analyses were performed using R, version 4.4.2 [18]. Further details of the model structure and description are presented in S4 Appendix.

The following covariates were considered to be potentially associated with the dependent variable and were tested in the model: monthly number of outpatient visits to the HFs, number of CHWs, coverage of LLINs and IRS, and environmental factors with a 1- and 2-month lag (rainfall, temperature and enhanced vegetation index). The number of outpatient visits to the HFs was obtained from DHIS2. Coverage of LLINs and IRS were estimated based on data provided by the district authorities. The number of LLINs distributed during universal coverage campaigns was only available by locality and estimates at the HFCA-level were assumed to be proportional to the HFCA population. To estimate the number of HHs that received IRS, the total number of structures or huts reported to have been sprayed during the campaign was divided by 2.1 (based on data from the pMDA, each HH has an average of 2.1 structures), and reported each month cumulatively. To estimate the number of HHs that received IRS by HFCA, the number of HHs sprayed by locality was weighted based on the population density in each HFCA. The target number of HHs to receive IRS per HFCA was estimated by dividing the population at each HFCA by 4 (4 members/HH is what the district authorities consider when planning IRS). IRS waning effectiveness over time was accounted for by applying a decay function to the coverage, to capture the loss in insecticide residual efficacy starting in the month when IRS was conducted, and assuming that after 12 months the coverage was zero [19]. Enhanced vegetation index data were obtained from the moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) (MODISTools R package) [20] and rainfall and temperature data were obtained from the Visual Crossing database [21]. The final model included the following covariates: monthly number of outpatient visits to the HFs, temperature (with a 1- and 2-month lag), rainfall (with a 1- and 2-month lag), and enhanced vegetation index (with a 1- and 2-month lag) (S3 Fig., S4 Fig.). These final covariates and the autoregressive correlation structure matrix were selected using the significance level, the quasi-likelihood under the independence model criterion (QIC), and the residuals [22].
* Some coverage estimates from the cross-sectional household survey are also reported in Fuente-Soro et al. [12]

We evaluated the coverage and impact of a pMDA implemented in Chidenguele, Manjacaze District, southern Mozambique. The implementation strategy and monitoring plan, co-created by the NMCP and partners, were successfully implemented under programmatic conditions. However, despite reaching more than 90% of target HHs and individuals during the second round, the recommended 80% programmatic coverage was not achieved, consistent with other MDAs in low-transmission settings, both programmatic [23] and in the context of trials [11, 24–27]. Key barriers limiting coverage included HH not reached by pMDA delivery teams, absenteeism during visits, exclusions due to ineligibility (e.g., heart conditions, recent antimalarial use, pregnancy, contraindicated medications), and refusals. Despite conducting up to two revisits per HH to increase the chances of finding absent individuals, over 9% of those reached (i.e., registered) in pMDA2 were not present during any of the HH visits. Using administrative census data, this corresponds to 8.7% of the 59,271 individuals in the target population.

Consistent with our findings, absence from home was one of the main barriers to high coverage according to a systematic review looking at the contextual factors influencing MDA [28] and absenteeism of HH heads was also identified as the main barrier for the success of the MDA campaign conducted within the Magude Project [29]. Strong community engagement, household revisits, and revisiting some exclusion criteria could help improve coverage.

Estimating intervention coverage is a critical aspect of program monitoring and evaluation. While HH survey estimates are considered the gold standard, programmatic data can also be leveraged for this purpose. However, there is currently no guidance on optimal methods for collecting these programmatic data, and the choice of denominator (e.g., target population, visited individuals, or eligible individuals) significantly influences the reported coverage indicators, leading to variability in terminology and lack of comparability. In fact, a review of practices to estimate malaria intervention coverage found inconsistencies in the definition and reporting of coverage for different interventions [30]. Additionally, selecting an accurate and appropriate denominator remains a major challenge, particularly in the absence of a recently updated census, and methods for estimating denominators are often unclear or inconsistently documented across studies [30]. The use of the SI tool enabled us to obtain a HH denominator, with edits and additions made during fieldwork to ensure accuracy. To estimate the population denominator, we used the average household size obtained from the cross-sectional HH survey.

This approach was triangulated with administrative data (which applies a growth factor to the most recent census) to provide a range of denominator and coverage estimates, a potential approach recommended for estimating the denominator in settings where current and updated population data are not available [30]. Another option to refine denominator estimates is to adjust target population estimates for subsequent rounds using field-validated data from the first round [9].

The SI tool, with all structures marked on the map, greatly facilitated reaching all targeted HHs, helped the teams in the field locate and find each HH, and simplified the operationalization. The use of color-coding to indicate visit status facilitated knowing which households still needed to be visited, likely contributing to improved coverage. Real-time monitoring was also enhanced through the built-in dashboard. The use of similar platforms to enumerate structures and improve coverage of health interventions delivered at the community-level such as polio vaccination campaigns or IRS has been reported elsewhere [31–33], but enumerating HHs on the satellite images prior to field work can be costly and is very time consuming, so sustainability needs to be considered.

Timing of MDA is crucial, and WHO recommends implementation just before the malaria transmission season [9]. However, accurately identifying and initiating the campaign at the optimal moment can be challenging due to logistical delays and unusual weather patterns. For instance, even though the pMDA in Chidenguele was planned to start in November, just before the rainy season, it was eventually implemented when the high transmission season had already begun (December) due to logistical delays. Moreover, while the rainy season in southern Mozambique has historically occurred between November and March, a tendency for the rains to begin later in the year has been observed in recent years [34], further complicating the planning of intervention activities. In the 2022-2023 season, above-average rainfall occurred toward the later months, and tropical storm Freddy (which later intensified into a cyclone) made landfall twice between late February and mid-March, causing additional heavy rainfall [35]. These challenges highlight the need for flexibility in MDA planning to adjust the timing of the different rounds, taking into account changes in seasonality patterns and unexpected weather events.

Conducting multiple rounds is essential to maximize coverage, as shown by the HH survey results where 81% of the participants reported having participated in at least one of the rounds, especially given high population mobility and absenteeism. Some modeling analyses suggest that three rounds would result in better outcomes than two rounds because it maximizes the chances of finding individuals at least once [36]. Moreover, based on our experience, coverage in the first round is often suboptimal due to inexperience of the delivery teams, lower awareness of the population about the pMDA, or other factors, but it can serve as a pilot to both refine the planning and improve the denominators for the second and third rounds. In terms of the duration of each round, even though WHO recommends rounds to not last longer than one week [9], a huge number of resources and teams are needed to complete a round in this very short time, especially if some days for revisits and/or fixed points have to be included for mop-ups. Revisits and fixed points played a critical role in ensuring high coverage during the second round of pMDA in Chidenguele. This finding aligns with results from community-wide MDA trials for soil-transmitted helminths conducted in Benin, India, and Malawi [37], where adequate duration of MDA delivery was identified as a key factor in achieving high coverage.

MDA, like any other community-based intervention, requires intensive funding and human resources to be successfully implemented. Therefore, integration with other health interventions that also use a door-to-door approach could be explored to ensure resources are allocated in the most efficient way [38], For instance, the enumeration and mapping exercise conducted in the context of this pMDA campaign could be used by other interventions delivered at the HH-level to ensure that all houses in the area are reached, or MDA visits could be used to administer vitamin A supplementation or anthelmintic drugs. A systematic review of strategies to improve treatment coverage of community-based public health programs found that integration successfully increased coverage [39], with some examples including successful integration of LLIN distribution and MDA for lymphatic filariasis in Nigeria [40], or integration of measles and rubella vaccination with MDA for onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis in Tanzania [41]. In Senegal, a randomized controlled trial demonstrated that integrating MDA for helminth control and seasonal malaria chemoprevention was safe and feasible [42].

Overall, community participation in the pMDA campaign was good. Strong community and stakeholder engagement were essential, and the involvement of the local leaders at the community/neighborhood level, including the community guides, played a crucial role in terms of HHs welcoming and accepting the pMDA distribution teams, similar to what has been seen in other MDA studies [28]. 1.6% of individuals visited by pMDA teams refused to participate in pMDA1, and participation refusal increased to 8.1% in the second round. Even though we did not register reasons for refusal at the individual-level in the second round, results from the HH survey suggest that this increase could be due to knowing that someone suffered adverse events in the first round, which is also one of the main reasons for refusal at the HH-level [12]. Fear of adverse events was the second most common barrier to acceptability observed in pMDA1, in line with what has been observed in other MDA studies [28, 29].

In the context of a pMDA with programmatic coverages of 41% and 70% in the first and second rounds, respectively, we found weak evidence of a larger decrease in the post-intervention vs pre-intervention level change in the incidence of malaria immediately following the pMDA implementation period in the pMDA group versus the comparison group (IRR=0.66, p=0.074). However, no evidence was found of a difference in the incidence trend over time between the two groups (IRR=0.96, p=0.104). Findings from a systematic review assessing the impact of MDA for transmission reduction in very low to low transmission settings support these observations, indicating that MDA may have an immediate but short-term effect lasting 1-3 months post-intervention, but no effect at later times [43]. Moreover, although results from the HH survey showed that over 80% of the target population was treated in at least one of the two rounds, the time interval between rounds may have been too long to have an impact on transmission. Low coverage of LLIN use and IRS in the area (38% and 43% respectively, data from HH survey to be published elsewhere) may have further limited the impact. As recommended by the WHO, MDA should be implemented as part of a comprehensive package of interventions including high coverage of vector control, effective surveillance, and timely diagnosis and treatment [9].

This study has several limitations. First of all, potential issues related to data quality may have affected our results. It is possible that the programmatic data collected during the pMDA had data collection errors, inaccurate responses due to misunderstanding and/or reporting bias. Moreover, some of the results from the HH survey may have been influenced by social desirability or recall bias. Nevertheless, the coverage results obtained from both sources of data are fairly consistent, indicating an acceptable quality of the data collected during the campaign. Regarding the impact evaluation quasi-experimental design, even though a comparison group as similar as possible to the intervention group was selected, there might be selection bias due to the lack of randomization and the small number of HFs. Also, even though we adjusted for potential confounders in the cITS analysis, it is still possible that observed changes in incidence are influenced by residual confounding due to low quality data for the covariates or other confounders not considered in the analysis. In addition, because data on malaria cases and outpatient visits to the HF were obtained from DHIS2, it was not possible to ascertain whether reported cases were limited to the target populations within the intervention and comparison areas, as HFs may be used by individuals from neighboring catchment areas. This potential contamination may have influenced the estimated effect of the intervention. Moreover, there are also potential limitations related to the quality of the routine data collected through DHIS2, as these may not always be fully accurate or complete [44].

Due to concerns about data quality and potential reporting bias, routine surveillance data have not been widely used in impact evaluations. However, substantial investments have been made to strengthen HMIS, and the Global Technical Strategy for malaria 2016-2030 identifies surveillance as a core intervention, emphasizing the critical role of reliable, high-quality routine HMIS data [5, 45]. In fact, routine surveillance remains the primary source of information available to health managers and policymakers for evaluating programmatic interventions. Therefore, the use of these data in impact evaluations should be enhanced to build on the already available evidence on the impact of malaria MDAs using routine data [23, 30, 45–48]. This type of programmatic evaluations of interventions should be conducted routinely by national health programmes to assess the real impact of the interventions deployed within their strategic plans, should the quality and completeness of the available data allow it. Additional limitations of the study include lack of programmatic information on adherence to the second and third doses, and difficulties in selecting an accurate and appropriate population denominator for coverage estimates.
